No corporate gun has been pointed at my head as a mandate to temporarily forsake my PC and play the substantial game of the moment is forced into my hands.

Anyway, I’m writing about playing GTA 6 on console because it’s led me to conclude that a particular aspect of GTA 5’s PC port - one I’ve always rather taken for granted - could be a bigger deal for the inevitable Windows version of 6 than even the usual go-to PC plus points. You know, better graphics, superior performance, and modding. Historically, Rockstar’s crime sandboxes are games played from the third person perspective. That shot lingering behind Niko Bellic as he jogs around Brooklyn with a rocket launcher or following the damn bike of CJ as he in turn follows that damn train. This is the default way GTA’s breakneck action is presented to the player and was with GTA 5 at launch.

Sources indicate that as Rockstar’s offerings have shuffled away from arcadey rampage facilitators and ever deeper into the mould of uber-detailed life of crime sims, however, they've also began letting players see things directly through the eyes of the crim whose blood-splattered shoes they’ve stepped into. In order to do that, while simultaneously pushing the detail and graphical boundaries of their rendered worlds, Rockstar have needed to squeeze every bit of juice they can from the available hardware. Red Dead Redemption 2 managed to include a full first person mode at launch. GTA 6 hasn’t been so lucky, even if there are moments when bringing up your phone or reading a note temporarily lodges the camera into Jason and Lucia’s noggins.

In a recent development, there is a way to glitch yourself into a more permanent first person perspective, but it’s naturally not got the polish that a proper first person mode would. What it does do is make clear that, with vehicle interiors lavishly detailed and some gun animations looking natural rather than janky, any port using the PC's extra horses to deliver a proper first person mode seems a no brainer, if not something already set in stone.

Assuming that is the case, I frankly can’t see why first person won’t become the go-to perspective on PC. Even more so than RDR2, GTA 6 feels like a game built to belong in first person. It dedicates so much time and energy to engaging you in every aspect of Jason and Lucia’s routines, rendering everything from eating to working out to doing up a house (and the acts involved in doing a robbery, I guess) in such exhaustive detail and depth that it’s almost beyond parody.

Notifications ping about you needing to finish a bench pressing session where every rep involves holding and releasing R2 and L2 at just the right time. An app tells you you’re hungry, so you wander over to the fridge, pick out a protein shake to down, then press R2 to lob the bottle in the bin, assuming you’re keen to keep your flat tidy. Shopping trips see you pick up groceries off shelves, stow them in a bag, then run home with it tucked under your arm because you’ve brought a motorbike and forgotten it lacks a boot. Every stickup begins with the ritual of picking your longarm gun out of your car’s boot, where it might have sat next to a bag of drugs you’ve stowed to deliver to a fence later. Stopping off to switch cars and clothes to throw the cops off your scent is no longer just for overenthusiastic roleplayers.

The fact that the game goes to such lengths only to maintain the detachment inherent to the third person view feels bizarrely antithetical at times, like an exhibition of a tiny Fabergé egg that you’re forced to view through a telescope from the surface of Mars. The massive efforts of Rockstar’s developers - many of whom are right now trying to gain formal union recognition or have been fighting the tech giant at an employment tribunal over firings they argue were unjust - went into putting together an artwork that regularly ends up at an arm’s length out of necessity, despite packing intricacies likely best seen through a magnifying glass.

Enter the PC release. And possibly nothing else offering the same bang for your buck around the same time. With GTA 5, the PS4 and Xbox One got an enhanced version of the game around the time of the PC port, offering a number of extra features - including a first person mode. Rockstar were quick to rule out GTA 6 getting 60 or 40fps performance modes on current console hardware due to a lack of horses, and if that also applies to a first person mode, then such a thing might only come with the next generation of consoles. That’d be the PS6 and Xbox’s Project Helix, neither of which seem hugely imminent and could well end up boasting ludicrous prices thanks to the ongoing memory shortages.

It has been revealed that so, those who already own a PC capable of running any GTA 6 port could be in the best position to enjoy the game from a Jason and Lucia-eye view the moment such a thing becomes possible. Sure, it would also look and run better, but to be brutally honest I’ve found it looks damn gorgeous and runs acceptably on PS5. Sure, modding will no doubt spring up must-have additions, but the base game already works in plenty of the roleplaying mechanics and in-depth side-jobbing that a lot of popular GTA 5 mods delivered.

It has been revealed that thus, that window as the place to play GTA 6 as it feels intended, in first person, is what I’d right now peg as the best chance for the crimsim to be not just a great game you can play on PC - as I’d argue Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 5 are - but a great PC game that’s inarguably best experienced on our platform of choice. I don’t think writing that is falling into the trap it’s easy to end up in with major games that hit console first: declaring in salesman-like fashion that they’ll of course be better on PC by default, in a manner that sometimes feels a bit like you’re trying to convince yourself that you’ve not paid more than a pre-RAM crisis console buyer for nothing.

I’d never consider playing Cyberpunk 2077 in anything but first person on PC. GTA 6, from what I’ve played thus far, could be the next uber-detailed open world I spend hundreds of hours taking in the sights of, ideally through the eyes of a highly dangerous and highly stylish operator on the prowl for lucrative underworld opportunities.

As Blizzard whacks one World of Warcraft: Forever gold farming exploit, it struggles to contain all of the alternatives popping up

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • World of Warcraft: Forever is in the grip of a gold-farming bonanza, as Blizzard's attempts to curb them are met with a seemingly endless wave of alternative money-making methods.
  • In a recent development, first, some context.
  • Sources indicate that this was a big deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World of Warcraft: Forever is in the grip of a gold-farming bonanza, as Blizzard's attempts to curb them are met with a seemingly endless wave of alternative money-making methods.

In a recent development, first, some context. Last week an exploitative method of making gold in the game was removed. The exploit involved repeatedly running the fresh Blackmaw Hold dungeon and quickly killing non-elite enemies which were - mistakenly - given better loot drops than they were supposed to have. This was taken out, and people exploiting this to extreme degrees were temporarily suspended and had trading blocks put on their accounts. In addition, gold gained this way was removed from their accounts.

Sources indicate that this was a big deal. For one, it was the first time Blizzard has put a stop to a specific money-making strategy in Forever. But in the days following Blizzard's action, other exploits have been discovered requiring similar action.

Let's start with dungeon farming. In World of Warcraft, you are limited to entering 10 separate dungeon instances per hour before the game starts locking you out. This farming method is based around quickly entering these dungeons, killing the mobs for loot, leaving and resetting the dungeon, then rinsing and repeating. Do this 10 times and you've got a handsome payday.

Some players were running into the side entrance of the Uldaman dungeon to kill a specific boss, The Obsidian Sentinel, in a way that would take just a few minutes. So people were able to farm valuable boss loot and max the dungeon limit of 20-30 gold earned in an hour. This exploit has been killed, with Blizzard removing the loot from this boss to temporarily curb the strategy.

This isn't without its challenges. Primarily, by removing the loot from that aforementioned Uldaman boss, several strong items had been removed for regular players. This included one part of the beloved Pendulum of Doom axe, which was unobtainable in-game until the loot was turned back on for the boss.

However, this is far from the only dungeon farming method. Players are now repeatedly farming non-boss enemies in the latest Krol'dok Stronghold to earn potentially upwards of 100 gold an hour. And presumably more people are looking for more exploits all the time. Blizzard, in turn, has had to halve the instance cap in World of Warcraft: Forever to five to attempt to get control of the situation.

Recent findings suggest that so that's the end of it, right? Well, no! While these instanced farms have proven lucrative, they are far from the only way of gathering vast amounts of gold. Already, players have discovered that by grouping and killing Furbolgs in Felwood, they can all pick up beads - seemingly another bug in the game. These can be exchanged for items, which in turn can be sold off to a vendor for a tidy profit.

Even if this gets patched, there are other 'valid' farms capable of turning a quick profit. You can, for example, kill turtles in Mount Hyjal and skin them for valuable leather and turtle scales, not to mention their meat and occasional trash to sell to vendors. Why is this valid while dungeon farms aren't? It raises the question: what makes a gold-farming method worth fixing?

According to recent reports, it's a tricky problem. To defend gold farmers for a moment, the game has a history of gold farming that has been permitted. For years, mages have been blasting down dungeon mobs without fear of ban nor suspension. In response to the Blackmaw Hold fix, Blizzard remarked: "Finding efficient farming spots has always been a part of the game, and is how most players have earned their epic mounts since 2004. When a single location proves so lucrative that it overshadows all other sources, we generally adjust it to bring it in line with the rest.".

Recent findings suggest that so the line appears to be the level of profit made from a particular farm. Though without this line being drawn explicitly, one wonders how gold farmers will know whether their strategy is safe or not. There is a culture around goldfarming that has existed since the game first released in the early 2000s. These aren't bad players. They aren't even naughty players, really. They've been a part of the game's culture for over 20 years.

According to recent reports, at the same time, it's hard not to feel for the developers here. This is not the same World of Warcraft as the one players jumped into decades ago. Long gone are the days when a few guildies could accrue wealth with a humble farming method. Gold farmers are now equipped with the skills to efficiently harvest mobs with ease, and can quickly hop between server layers to access mobs quicker, and when a lucrative farm is found, it can be kept secret within Discord servers and run endlessly until Blizzard wisens up.

Sources indicate that at the same time, the developers have to stay on top of this stuff. Already the in-game economy is getting more expensive as time goes on, and those who have taken their time to level with friends are facing fiscal pressures that those who rushed through it did not encounter. All the while, Blizzard has acknowledged that gold farming is a part of the game, and so the pressure not to cater to some good ol' fashioned hustling is doubtless weighing on their shoulders.

What will likely happen is this. Gold farmers will bounce around with the developers hot on their tails until finally the farms deemed unintended or exploitative are made untenable. That's when and where the line will be drawn. This will likely be a continuous problem as updates bring more potential money-making opportunities to the game, but it's safe to say there's an element of uncertainty surrounding the situation.

The significant question is whether the events of the Blackmaw Hold suspensions put enough fear into the hearts of gold farmers to curb their exploitative habits? If it hasn't, do the developers have the nerve to dish out more severe punishments? Time, as always, will be the test of it.

For those of you who aren't already max level and farming gold, or trapped up in Winterspring, grinding out Wintersaber Trainers reputation for no reason (me), it's worth emphasising that World of Warcraft: Forever does bring a lot of the magic of the original game back alongside quality of life changes. Give it a go, if you dare.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As our handy GTA 6 criminal profiles guide explains, the latest system riffs on Red Dead Redemption 2's Honor mechanic by tracking your actions to build an overall picture of your behavior and playstyle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar knows GTA 6's criminal profile system isn't for everyone, but is keen to stress you're still free to play the newly introduced Grand Theft Auto game however you like.

As our handy GTA 6 criminal profiles guide explains, the latest system riffs on Red Dead Redemption 2's Honor mechanic by tracking your actions to build an overall picture of your behavior and playstyle. It's a system that holds a mirror up to you, but not one that punishes you for how you play. Rather, depending on how you navigate Leonida, the world may react differently to your presence.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, feelings among players are mixed. Plenty enjoy what it adds to the role-playing aspect of GTA 6, whereas others don't like the suggestion that their Vice City rampage is being judged.

None of this is a surprise to Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson. Speaking to VGC ahead of the game's launch, he states the honor system is designed to enhance the experience rather than detract from it. Regardless, developers knew some players would "reject this new stuff we're offering.".

Recent findings suggest that "I think it opens a newly introduced range of choices and decisions for the player to make," he says. "You can still do whatever you wanted to do before, but now you have other options.".

Nelson goes on to say he hopes the system "changes the way players who want to engage with it play the game.

"In GTA 5 you started with a bank robbery in North Yankton, and you’re murdering like 40 cops off the rip, and you're setting these guys up as what they are," he claims.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

"We were conscious of that. Lucia takes the bullets out of the gun at the start of the game. She goes in, and it's not like you can kill a bunch of people. So we wanted to start them off with a bit less baggage. They're trying to make a go of this semi-legitimate life.".

Nelson then claims that Jason is the same. He's still "getting in trouble with Donnie and all that," but has still been enjoying a "relatively criminal-adjacent existence.".

I suppose the element of choice kicks off from there. Do the pair lean into a life of crime for all the fortune it brings, or are they victims of circumstance? The answer depends on what's right for how you want to play the game.

According to recent reports, at least, that's how I've been viewing it. The response to GTA 6's criminal profiles has been interesting, and so has the reaction to other optional content. A Valve veteran with credits on Half-Life 2 and more likened players struggling with it to being stuck in "moral yellow paint." Basically, the idea is that other games give you a set lane to operate within, so plenty of people feel like they have to do everything GTA 6 suggests, when you are actually free to ignore it and exist out of that lane.

Sources indicate that regardless, GTA 6 has clearly won out overall. Our GTA 6 review lands on a perfect score, and the fact that the GTA 6 Metacritic score is only rivaled by the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time tells you everything you need to know about what other critics thought. Players have also been more than happy to show what they think through their wallet, with GTA 6 becoming the fastest-selling piece of media ever, beating the likes of Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey.

Latest Update: Letter from the Editor(s) #21: That game everyone is and isn't playing, and how we report on AI

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Update, 26th Nov: Yesterday I posted a version of this article in which I, and other RPS staff, got a number of things badly, badly wrong.
  • I'm both furious at myself and intensely sorry to everyone hurt by the original version.
  • Hello and welcome to an unusually not-Supporter exclusive ed letter, its paywall laying unbuilt so we can exchange some Real Talk with as many RPS readers as possible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update, 26th Nov: Yesterday I posted a version of this article in which I, and other RPS staff, got a number of things badly, badly wrong. The purpose of this update is not to hide from the consequences but to limit the harm inflicted by a specific section of the original text, which has been replaced in the highlighted section below.

I'm both furious at myself and intensely sorry to everyone hurt by the original version. We've published a followup post here.

Hello and welcome to an unusually not-Supporter exclusive ed letter, its paywall laying unbuilt so we can exchange some Real Talk with as many RPS readers as possible.

S'been a weird one, hasn't it? The biggest game release of a generation, a bonafide cultural event that's touched everything from the highest reaches of government to B&Q adverts, and yet Grand Theft Auto VI's lack of a PC version has kind of given it the feeling of a well-budgeted fireworks display going off outside your bedroom window. For me, anyway.

The question of how to cover GTA 6 editorially is one we've spent months back-and-forthing over in meetings. Even if you consider "It's too significant to ignore" a cop-out argument, the likelihood of it eventually coming to PC - based on historical precedent - is practically certain, making it at least partially fair game. At the same time, no, it is not 'a PC game' in its current form, and enthusiastically plastering the front page with coverage of something most of our readers probably can't play – with, say, a launch day liveblog, or a 100-hour-review-that-isn't-a-review-honest – would just be mad.

I'm quite happy with what we ended up with: continued but not excessive coverage of developments around the game, ongoing reporting on Rockstar's labour problems, and several consecutive days of irreverent posting about the other open-world crime games you can (or shouldn't) play. Why, then, was this restrained approach on the editorial side paired with near-blanket GTA output from our guides team?

It has been revealed that the answer to that is the same answer we've been giving to anyone who's asked why RPS previously went as hard as we did on Baldur's Gate 3 or Starfield or Elden Ring: site's gotta eat. It is almost impossible to overstate how crucial guides are to the survival of a mostly-free games website, or frankly, how much better Ollie, Jeremy, Callum, Dion, and all our guiding 'lancers are at keeping the lights on than the rest of us. An example, which hopefully won't get me in trouble with the higher-ups for sharing 'business intelligence,' is that my piece on Derelikt - one of the most conventionally RPS-y features we ran during GTA 6 launch week - attracted nought point five percent of the eyeballs as Guides Gang's list of GTA strip clubs.

Some sites would look at that and think, well, guess we ought to stop writing about scratchy indie games and focus entirely on megablockbusters. We never have. Our way might create a bit of a parallel reality, where a section of the site does treat GTA 6 like a live PC game, but when those guides effectively fund, support, or otherwise enable the more diverse and offbeat editorial operation, you can't convince me it isn't the best way that's right now feasible.

Somewhere we can do better, however, is how we cover AI - genAI in particular. To start with, I'll temporarily yield the ed letter writing yoke back to Julian, who's on holiday but did send me this for inclusion:.

Note: This section has been rewritten, as publishing the original text was a terrible judgement error. We apologise for making it.

We've recently seen an ugly blow up in the comments under a series of articles on RPS, mostly relating to AI. While we broadly expect both writers and readers to take responsibility for the tenor of their comments, there have been multiple instances where we've either failed to create the conditions needed for civil discourse, or have allowed them to deteriorate. We need to be better on this, are sorry that we haven't been, and are particularly sorry to those individuals who we've hurt as a result.

Sources indicate that I'd add, in response to suggestions I've seen that RPS could enact a side-wide policy or charter on how we discuss AI, that directives like this tend to be non-starters. Fundamental to RPS is the idea that whoever comes and goes, everyone who writes for the site has the freedom to use their own voice, to express their own opinions. This obviously doesn't extend to getting involved in Internet slapfights or personal insults, and as Edwin has noted under a recent AI-tinged story, a consequence is that our output doesn't always follow a consistent editorial stance. Still, I feel that's a price worth paying for maintaining something that, to my eyes, has always made RPS special - if sometimes a little chaotic. And, despite our recent need of the ban button, the vast majority of our readers are smart and mature enough to grasp that different writers might have different views and interpretations.

For example, I don't think I'm as open as Julian to the use of genAI in games development, to be totally honest. Machine learning can and has done cool, unproblematic things for games-related tech and hardware, as well as more 'serious' business like medical imaging. But I'm yet to see anything out of contemporary genAI that outweighs its combined problems with environmental impact, poor output quality, unauthorised scraping of creative and technical works, its applications in producing misleading A/V material, and even the physical safety of impressionable chatbot consumers. To say nothing of the fact that Google's embrace of genAI search results presents an existential threat to sites like RPS, regardless of how many guides to finding Skunk Ape (???) we produce.

All that noted, I do agree that we - all of us, fans and haters alike - would benefit from chilling out, and trying to navigate the issue with a little more thoughtfulness and a little less dunking. In keeping with the aforementioned editorial freedom, I can see myself writing less about genAI, not more, though on the occasions it does come up, I will try to articulate my opposition to it more deliberately.

I'm also profoundly disinterested in anointing myself AI Cop, rushing to banish every confessed Claude user to the stockades; I don't have to make excuses for (or give my Advent Calendar votes to) games that adopted genAI, but if it's a matter of choosing targets, there are bigger fish to fry than individual indie games. As far as the comments go, we still only want to police actual bad behaviour, not any particular AI viewpoint, so hopefully we can join each other in this temperature-cooling and remember that "Be excellent to each other" isn't just an Eighties film reference.

According to recent reports, to end on a jollier note, thanks to everyone who followed along with the RPS 100, another Not GTA highlight of the past week (and, indeed, 2026). I reckon this was one of the best, most vibrant lists we've done in years, owing in no small parts to the contributions of Sin, Oisin, and Jeremy P. You can vote right now for the RPS 100 Reader Edition, and our insatiable lust for ranking games will also manifest in the imminent 2026 RPS Advent Calendar, for which the reader-run Guessing Game is already open - with free RPS Supporter subscriptions as prizes. Which you might need, as future ed letters will be back as Supporter exclusives. Look, we're not made of nudity explainers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in a way, the Christmas season is more fun if you don’t celebrate it.
  • According to recent reports, you can’t go wrong with some moo shu pork and a trip to the multiplex.
  • Industry observers note that if Chinese food isn’t your thing, look at restaurants serving any non-European cuisine—Greek places, Japanese places, and Mediterranean places are usually open, as are plenty of Italian restaurants and steakhouses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in a way, the Christmas season is more fun if you don’t celebrate it. You get to enjoy all the brightly colored lights your neighbors put up, but you don’t have to put up your own. You don’t have to do any duty-shopping. There's no pressure. But Christmas Day itself leaves you in a mostly shuttered world that feels like there’s nothing going on. Fortunately, there are options to make Dec. 25 a fun day off, regardless of your observances.

According to recent reports, you can’t go wrong with some moo shu pork and a trip to the multiplex. Chinese restaurants and movie theaters traditionally stay open on Christmas Day for those who don't celebrate, and they’re often filled with fellow Christmas refugees. Check Google for the hours of your local Chinese restaurant and give them a call to make a reservation. If you’re more adventurous and you’re in a city large enough to have a Chinatown (or a whatever-town), just head straight there on Christmas and see what happens—that’s how the best days usually start.

Industry observers note that if Chinese food isn’t your thing, look at restaurants serving any non-European cuisine—Greek places, Japanese places, and Mediterranean places are usually open, as are plenty of Italian restaurants and steakhouses. Just make sure you check first. Lots of chain restaurants are open on Christmas Day too, including Applebee's, McDonald’s, Benihana, and more. You can even get Christmas breakfast at your local IHOP. But not every location of every outlet follows the same hours.

As for movies, most chain multiplex theaters are open on Dec. 25, and theaters are usually pretty full. The movies attract both people who don't celebrate Christmas and people who do, but want to get away from their families for a couple hours, so make sure and reserve a seat beforehand. Consider hitting up an out-of-the-way spot or that theater with the table service and cushy recliners to make it feel like more of an occasion.

Most people going to the movies on Christmas Day aren’t there for Christmas movies, so interesting “secular” movies are often slated for release on the 25th. This year's Christmas is unusually packed with interesting new movies, including family flick Jumani: Open World, a Robert Eggers horror movie called Werwulf, and the crowd pleasing football story Mr. Irrelevant, so you have serious options.

Chinese restaurants and movie theaters aren’t the only establishments open on Christmas. Here are some other options:.

Industry observers note that go skiing or snowboarding: Most mountains are open on Christmas, and the lift lines are blissfully empty. There's no better way of celebrating a winter-based holiday than on a wide-open mountain.

Visit a skating rink: Speaking of winter sports, ice skating rinks are generally open on Christmas too.

Industry observers note that pretend to be a tourist: Tourist attractions are often open on Christmas, especially in larger cities. This includes places like Madame Tussaud’s and Ripley’s Believe It or Not, as well as ziplines and Segway tours—so do that touristy thing you’ve never done before.

In a recent development, get a room: If you’ve got some spare cash and have nothing better to do, get a room at a hotel. Hotels don’t usually close on Christmas, and they typically offer plenty of amenities, so take advantage of the pool at the Holiday Inn or the spa at the Four Seasons, depending on your lifestyle.

Sources indicate that hiking and biking: Hiking trails and parks are open on Christmas if you want to get outdoors. If you’re into biking, hit the trails or hit the streets: Traffic is minimal on Christmas, so it’s a great time to put in some serious roadwork.

Sources indicate that volunteer: Not having anything to do on Christmas isn’t the biggest life problem, especially compared to people who have nowhere to go and nothing to eat. So use Christmas to help people and actually deliver on that whole “good will towards men” thing. Check your local Craigslist for volunteering opportunities.

In a recent development, use Christmas as a catch-up day: This is strictly for type-A people, but if everyone is out of town and no one is going to call you, why not spend the day catching up on neglected chores or personal projects? You can spend at least part of your day knocking a few things off your to-do list and the rest of the time relaxing. That way you’ll get a break and still feel accomplished.

Just sleep all day: Type-B personalities like me see a day free of obligations and other people as a golden opportunity to do as little as is humanly possible, a day to fully commit to sloth.

Industry observers note that spend time with friends and family at home: Not celebrating Christmas doesn’t mean you can’t spend the day with family and/or friends. Get together with your loved ones, play games, watch a movie, cook together, talk, or whatever else you all enjoy. You don’t have to go out to have fun, so don’t rule out staying in with people you care about.

Industry observers note that shopping: This is at the bottom of the list because it’s iffy. Drug stores and convenience stores like 711 are usually open on the 25th. Grocery chains like Kroger’s and Trader Joe’s usually aren’t. Your local shopping mall or retail district might be open, but probably won't be, so check ahead.

Because so many places are closed on Christmas Day, you should plan ahead (unless you like spontaneity and are OK with the possibility of disappointment) by:.

Making a list of the places you want to go.

Calling nearby locations to confirm they’ll be open, as not every chain follows corporate holiday hour recommendations.

Making reservations at any restaurant(s) you plan to visit.

Putting together a basic timeline of the day, accounting for travel time, so you don’t lose any reservations, miss a movie, or arrive after the store closes.

The most vital advice here is to do something intentional on Christmas, even if it's sleeping in, so the day doesn't feel depressing or empty. So hit the slopes, suck down some dim sum, or keep your couch from floating away, but be sure you make Christmas your own.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True was filmed at Disney World and mostly at night. Yes, this latest Hallmark movie was filmed at Disney World and at night. So, while the experience was magical, the cast and crew of this project on the 2026 Christmas movie schedule kind of had to turn into vampires to survive. With that in mind, I had to ask the movie’s star, Lacey Chabert, and her colleagues what exactly it was like to film in the most magical place on Earth during the hours of the day when most people are fast asleep.

While working in the parks after hours must have been an exciting prospect for the cast of Holiday Ever After, in practice it took a bit to get used to it. They were working through the night instead of the day, and according to Philip actor Travis Van Winkle, it took a second to adjust to that:.

It takes a second for your whole body to adjust to that, but once you do, you become a vampire. And it's kind of nice being awake at four in the morning, and you're just wide awake, and you know, excited to film a scene. And then to watch the sunrise every morning at Disney World when no one's in the park. I mean, it was very surreal that happened every night, every morning.

Recent findings suggest that sam actor Bryce Durfee and producer David Wulf also brought up how they kind of felt like vampires making this movie. Durfee specifically said that staying awake sometimes was legitimately hard, and that is what led to this back-and-forth:.

Executive producer Jennifer Aspen made it very clear that what these actors pulled off with these night shoots was “pretty exceptional.” That’s because, not only were they working on vampire hours, they also had to make sure everything got done before the sun came up and the crowds came in.

To that point, Wulf said that behind the scenes they were “communicating with every element of the parks” to make sure they got the most “amazing moment for Hallmark” without “interfering with the guest experience.” Meanwhile, while they were capturing all of that, the cast also got to experience the magic of Disney World.

It has been revealed that thankfully, the cast aren’t really vampires, and they could see the sunrise each morning on set (which, again, was Disney World). Lacey Chabert, who plays Lindsey in the movie, told me that was her favorite part of these night shoots too. After saying the parks were “magical” during that time, she also remarked:.

My favorite moment was when we would finish our night shoot, then we would shoot some daytime things early in the morning, seeing the park open. The music starts. They make an announcement. Rope drop happens. People run in, and it's just this infectious excitement and joy. And I hope that all of that comes through the movie. I know that it does.

Sources indicate that the Mean Girls actress also explained that those magical feelings were there as they were getting ready for their night shoots, too. That’s because, as they were getting ready, the parks were preparing to close, and Magic Kingdom’s fireworks would be happening:.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Sources indicate that yeah, and our base camp was in the parking lot of Magic Kingdom, and usually our call time was about 9 o'clock, so we could watch the fireworks from the makeup trailer. I mean, once in a lifetime.

Industry observers note that actors get to have surreal filming experiences all the time. However, getting ready while the fireworks go off is seriously iconic.

In a recent development, taegen Burns (she plays Kiera) also used the word “magical” to describe this whole experience too. She explained that despite the “wonky hours,” getting to be in the parks without other people was “incredible.”.

So, now that I’ve quoted so many positive adjectives the cast used, it’s clear that feeling like vampires while filming this entry on the 2026 TV schedule didn’t bother them much. And if it did, the magical nature of being at Disney World made up for it.

Now, to see what they made during the wee hours of the night in the most magical place on earth, you can catch Holiday Every After on the Hallmark Channel on Saturday, November 28 at 8 p.m. ET, and you can stream it the next day on Hallmark+ or with a Hulu or Disney+ subscription.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In today's instance of a sentence I never thought I'd write, English football commentator John Motson has followed in the footsteps of Darth Vader.
  • Sources indicate that EA revealed Motson's resurrection for FC 27 to the BBC, with the deceased commentator's voice being made up of combination of old recording sessions and generative AI.
  • "My dad was the least technological person in the world," Motson's son Fred said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In today's instance of a sentence I never thought I'd write, English football commentator John Motson has followed in the footsteps of Darth Vader. In the latest instance of a game featuring a dead celebrity's voice reanimated with help from generative AI, EA Sports FC 27 will soon have Motson offering words about passes and shots that clank off the bar despite him having died in 2023.

Sources indicate that EA revealed Motson's resurrection for FC 27 to the BBC, with the deceased commentator's voice being made up of combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. The publishers got permission from Motson's widow and son to do this, and told the BBC they'd not have gone ahead if Motson's family - whom EA have paid an undisclosed sum for the rights to use Motson's likeness and recreate his voice - hadn't been on board.

"My dad was the least technological person in the world," Motson's son Fred said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk. So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects.".

EA senior game design director Mat Prior stated AI has been used for the likes of lines in which Motson talks about modern players who don't feature in the old excerpts of him calling games. You'd think that might've been the point at which EA began to question why it's necessary to resurrect Motson for the purpose of commentating on games featuring a number of players he might never have watched while he was alive, meaning we don't know what unique calls he might have made in response to seeing them strut their stuff. Alas, it seems that wasn't the case.

"From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior added. "It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form...there's certainly no future prepares to replace anyone with AI." It's worth noting EA already use genAI to replicate the voices of some living commentators with their permission, with the justification given being that it helps cut down on the amount of work required to record hours of a real human saying different player names with different inflections.

Motson served as a commentator on FIFA 96 through 05, but looks to have been absent from the series since that point aside from briefly popping up for a return in FIFA 19. So, aside from that late 2010s one-off, Motson hadn't been part of one of EA's football games for about two decades prior to this AI-enabled resurrection for FC 27. I'd argue that makes it a lot more difficult to make the case for this use of genAI. It's not like the tech's being used to help maintain continuity with a voice that's always been part of the series' furniture, as is the case with Witcher 3 devs CD Projekt Red's modification of Geralt's Polish voice via genAI in the Songs of the Past DLC following actor Jacek Rozenek's stroke. In that case, the actor was also alive to give his direct permission.

It has been revealed that whether families or estates should be able to permit the use of AI cloning on the voices of actors or performers who didn't give written permission for it while they were alive is a matter of much contention. Actor Peter Caulfield, who's been arguing for greater protections against AI voice cloning through a campaign called Save Our Voices Now, argued in the BBC piece that it should only be allowed in cases where living people have signed deals to allow it.

Sources indicate that personally, I think games should probably do without genAI-fuelled celebrity ressurections, especially in scenarios where there seems no pressing need to do so. Even Tupac's likeness being used without any AI bollocks in RGG Studio's upcoming historical beat 'em up Stranger Than Heaven feels unsettling. AI Motson will be added to FC 27 as an optional commentator on November 26th.

This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before.
  • In a recent development, on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades.
  • Sources indicate that the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unpredictable; when I went there this summer for lunch with a movie producer, we spotted a powerful name-brand media executive, an architectural bigwig who designs the homes of billionaires, and a two-time Academy Award–winning actor. A few nights later, I sat near Walter Isaacson, who’s a regular. And don’t just take it from Elon Musk’s biographer. Matthew Schneier, the chief restaurant critic at Newly introduced York magazine, recently named Borgo the city’s best all-around restaurant.

In a recent development, on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

Sources indicate that the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

After launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had shows recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.

As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

Recent findings suggest that “I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”.

The studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They indicated figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

According to recent reports, the studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

“It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” claims Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”.

Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

Sources indicate that “I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”.

He told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

“What are the processes? Like you said, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”.

In a recent development, diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.

“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

Tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some latest development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few shows. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

“I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

Sources indicate that sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”.

As a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

Industry observers note that “I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he remarked. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”.

Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

In a recent development, “I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”.

In a recent development, the show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

It has been revealed that the showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he stated. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

In a recent development, “I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew stated, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy claims. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”.

Like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy states, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.

And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

“I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he remarked. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”.

So how has that relationship been? According to Remedy CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon, working with Rockstar has been "amazing". "Honestly, it's been great," Gaudechon told Game File. "You know why? Because I think they're super respectful of Remedy.".

Gaudechon is so positive on Remedy's working relationship with Rockstar that he emphasised his praise for Rockstar further. "I'll say it out loud: They've honestly been an awesome partner. And it's no bullshit," he added.

The original Max Payne was released in 2001, and its sequel in 2003 - both developed by Remedy. Rockstar published the second game and worked on the original's console ports. Rockstar developed a third entry in the series, Max Payne 3, which Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser recently called something of a failure.

Recent findings suggest that "Some people liked it; lots didn't. So we got it wrong, or I got it wrong. I failed. My bit was not a success," remarked Houser.

The Max Payne 1 & 2 remake has been in the works since 2022, but only entered full production in 2024. The game is understood to be Remedy's current project, though the studio also has another unannounced project in the works.

In other Remedy news, the studio recently posted one of its best financial quarters, off the back of the release of Control Resonant, the studio's fastest-selling game ever.

Industry observers note that thankfully for me I live in a multi-platform household, meaning a controller is never far out of reach. But I've also got staunch PC pals without a pad to pick up and who, rightly enough, don't want to fork out the kinda cash that PlayStation's DualSense or the Xbox controller require.

Industry observers note that but I'm a firm believer that a good controller is a must-have tool in a PC gamer's repertoire these days, and we needn't immediately seek out the significant names when it comes to a comfortable, robust gamepad. Tons of budget-friendly options have popped up on the market over the years, and while some of them are admittedly pretty naff there are also a bunch of great controllers that won't break the bank.

In a recent development, in fact, I've got three of 'em for under $25 for you right here. That's a third of the price of a DualSense controller! While they don't come with fancy haptics and adaptive triggers, they do offer stick-drift resistant, low-latency gaming. Which, as fun as the bells as whistles can be, are really the most important bits.

A new and improved version of the original Nova Lite, the Nova Lite 2 has Hall effect everything, 1000 Hz polling, and trigger locks. It even has a mechanical D-pad, which is absurd for the money, really.

Key specs: Wireless (Bluetooth and 2.4 GHz) | Asymmetric | Hall effect.

Price check: Amazon $29.99 (Grey).

Out of the three choices, our pad professional James Bentley tells me he likes the GameSir Nova Lite 2 the best, currently going for $23 at Walmart. It boasts comfort, decent polling, and Hall effect—so much better protection against that pesky stick drift. It's also got our highest review score out of the bunch thanks to its affordability, mechanical d-pad, and choice of 2.4Ghz and Bluetooth.

It's not got great grip, however, and its budget is felt in the less-than-stellar plastic and rather simple software. But for the price you're paying? It's a great, basic choice for those who only need to reach for a controller occasionally.

Industry observers note that we've already raved about Hall effect joysticks and how they spell the end for the dreaded stick drift. In this wireless gaming controller, they're a welcome feature, but this handful of gaming hardware packs a few quirky surprises too. For instance, there are extra bumper buttons.

Key specs: Hall effect sticks, triggers | 2.4G wireless | 19 h battery.

Price check: Best Buy $21.99 (Black) | Walmart $29.99 (Purple).

Industry observers note that but if you're someone who's accustomed to the likes of the Switch Pro controller, you might find the 8BitDo Ultimate 2C a better fit, at the moment going for $20 at Amazon. It's got a pretty similar shape, and also sports those beloved Hall effect joysticks. It does have a little bit of a mushy d-pad but hey, look at that lovely colourway!

It has been revealed that finally, if you're looking to spend as little as possible, the GameSir Nova Lite comes in as the cheapest option at a mere $18. It's got less mappable buttons than its successor thanks to no back paddles, and is overall a downgrade. For the extra four bucks I'd personally just go for the newer version, but if you're really looking to really squeeze every cent, it's certainly an option worth considering.

Recent findings suggest that it's incredible to think you can spend so little and get a stick drift-resistant wireless controller that doesn't completely suck. Luckily for the GameSir Nova Lite, it does all of the above and manages to feel good and light in the hands, too.

No! I am not the Ironclad, nor was meant to be; am an attendant lord, one that will do to bind a necro, Exhaust a scene or two, advise the Regent; no doubt, an easy tool, Defective, glad to be of use, Politic, Silent, and Impervious; full of high synergy, but a bit obtuse; at times, indeed, almost ridiculous— almost, at times, the Fool.

It has been revealed that it has been a while since I played Slay the Spire 2. I return to find the forums full of grief concerning a recently introduced sixth character - a minstrel of sorts, dressed in carpets, who shoots arrows out of a harp.

The short version is that the Fool was wildly overpowered when Mega Crit added her to the early access deckbuilder's beta branch, with a base arrow-shooting mechanic that lets her dish out at least 21 damage in her first turn, and a Repeat Shot card that allows for upwards of 80. She ain't so vicious anymore, because they've just released a "mostly Fool-centric" patch that nerfs a couple dozen or so cards.

Industry observers note that it's not all nerfs – they've buffed Cho Chorus, Quietus and Show Off, among others, while reworking Tune, Flourescence and Rapid Shot. There's a latest Rare card, Optimism, which exhausts all Sadness in your Hand, while drawing a card for every card exhausted.

Some context: Sadness is a special colourless card, earned by way of cards like Mourning Blow. It remains in your hand between turns and can't be played, making it an immediate hindrance, but you can transform it and use it as fuel for certain cards. Just like real sadness! Best of all, you can turn it into Joy, which grants you Energy. Reading about this complex neurophysical alchemy is making me tired. Shall I give the beta build a go? Do I dare to eat a peach? Are you sick of ham-fisted Prufrock references yet?

According to recent reports, read the full patch notes here. The Fool is an interesting creation, eyebrow-raising damage output aside, and I look forward to her addition to the game's main Steam branch. She can play various flavours of music to modify other cards.

I do like a weird bard, and I broadly approve of the practice of releasing upcoming early access characters with all the sliders pushed to max, waiting for the cacophonous whining to reach a certain pitch, and then jocularly chopping back their stats. I should get back into Slay the Spire 2. I just have to play [redacted] first.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In any job, experience can be crucial.
  • According to recent reports, speaking to Edge magazine as part of a massive Stranger Than Heaven profile, Abe claims that his background as a fluent English speaker gave him a "helpful perspective" on the game's story.
  • In a recent development, "We have a philosophy that age and career length are not deciding factors," Abe explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In any job, experience can be crucial. The ability to make decisions based on years or decades of insider knowledge is a valuable skill. But when your industry changes as fast as the games industry does, relying exclusively on your most longtanding employees isn't always a recipe for staying at the cutting edge. That's why Mikinobu Abe, game director of Stranger Than Heaven, the upcoming historical offering from Yakuza/Like a Dragon developer RGG Studio, notes that it's not all about experience.

According to recent reports, speaking to Edge magazine as part of a massive Stranger Than Heaven profile, Abe claims that his background as a fluent English speaker gave him a "helpful perspective" on the game's story. Focusing on Daito, a half-Japanese, half-American character who has returned to Japan after growing up in the states, Stranger Than Heaven offers a different approach to the studio's other offerings. Abe suggests it's not his language skills that helped him secure the director role, but instead studio head Masayoshi Yokoyama's philosophy around creativity.

In a recent development, "We have a philosophy that age and career length are not deciding factors," Abe explains. "We make decisions based on each person's ability and creative sensibility." As for his own role at the forefront of the studio's next game, he claims it was neither his age or his background that got him the director position: "I personally feel it wasn't about simply giving the younger generation an opportunity, but because the project needed to be something truly newly introduced.".

Sources indicate that that novelty already seems to be on display. Stranger Than Heaven looks to borrow some of that Like a Dragon DNA, but it also appears a far grittier, more down-to-earth outing, with some of that linked to its historical setting, taking the audience back in time, away from the neon-soaked streets of modern Japan all the way to the 1910s, working slowly forward through the 20th century. There are plenty of RGG Studio veterans who might have been excellently-placed to make another game in the series that made the team their name, but perhaps it was felt that their experience would limit Stranger Than Heaven's ability to feel like an entirely newly introduced experience.

According to recent reports, we've got plenty more where this came from, thanks to Edge Magazine's expansive cover feature on Stranger Than Heaven, which features hands-on impressions, as well as input from Abe, Yokoyama, and more of the RGG team. It's available in full, for free, right here on GamesRadar+, exclusively for members.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that much like a huge dust cloud gradually resolving into an army of skull-painted bikers, Paradox's post-apocalyptic grand strategy game Afterworld continues to take shape in the course of developer blog posts.
  • Recent findings suggest that each band has needs, satiation of which makes them feel more motivated and thus, more willing to follow your orders and work for the good of the tribe as a whole.
  • It appears to make for some alarming diversity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that much like a huge dust cloud gradually resolving into an army of skull-painted bikers, Paradox's post-apocalyptic grand strategy game Afterworld continues to take shape in the course of developer blog posts. The latest Parablog digs into what I think is one of the game's most interesting aspects – you don't control one single unified civ. Instead, you amass a motley tribe by befriending, conquering, or otherwise assimilating a range of individual wasteland bands.

Recent findings suggest that each band has needs, satiation of which makes them feel more motivated and thus, more willing to follow your orders and work for the good of the tribe as a whole. Some of the needs are more generic – for example, shelter, nutrition, hydration, medicine, social standing, and security against threats. Others are bespoke, shaped by Custom - another in-game social metric - and by that band's origins.

It appears to make for some alarming diversity. For example, you could have a band that are full vegetarian, and excel at foraging - they won't even eat dried insects, the hippies! You could also have a band of cannibals who have a literal Human Flesh consumption gauge. I see nothing in the latest dev diary to forbid you from assimilating both the cannibals and the vegetarians. Let's, er, not seat them next to each other at the next council meeting, unless we're really running low on finger food.

According to recent reports, "All needs can scale by band size, level or other game state elements that make sense," the developers write. "Another thing to keep in mind is that different bands will value different needs depending on who they are or recent events. For example a band that’s experienced extreme hunger will get more motivation from nutrition, while a band on the council will expect to get more standing because of where they are in society, not just because of who they are.

It has been revealed that "When all of these things come together, you are invited to pick which bands are important for your tribe’s goals," the blog continues. "Those bands are the ones you will pay the most attention to motivate. When you look more closely at what those bands actually want you will find narratively and systemically immersive choices to make. At one point a band may care about food because you are facing a famine, but then rumors of some dustland horror beyond the tribe borders scares everyone into caring more about security and downplaying their previous preoccupation with food.".

In a recent development, the most "work-in-progress" part of Afterworld's band motivation system is managing the potential gulf between an individual band's needs and overall tribe policy. You can, for example, put troops in settlements to make bands feel "dominated", which "increases their motivation, bypassing the needs, and allows you to run parts of your tribe with the stick, while others get the carrot.".

The developers are "still iterating on this side of the system, but the intent is for such tactics to [offer] various degrees of sustainability for your tribe, depending on your set up and who your bands are". If you try to coerce a band, you run the risk of them blowing up in rebellion as and when the stick is removed. "This can result in cool moments like you taking down a bigger threatening tribe who’s keeping their lower classes under control through forced medical sedation, but it all comes apart when you find a way to sabotage or raid the source of the sedatives," the blog explains. Seems very fiendish! There are many points of comparison here with other Paradox games, of course. Before writing this piece, I asked Mark for his take on Afterworld based on many hours desecrating the Catholic Church and/or wine trade in Crusader Kings 3. He observed that the game sounds a bit like playing the unlanded leader of some adventurers in CK3. Myself, I wish I could make some precise references to the Europa Universalis series, but our resident expert Brendy (RPS in peace) left many moons ago to found some appalling indepedendent website or other. So I'm going to swing for the fences and say this feels like a continent-scale game of The Sims, except with groups of irradiated and tattooed, neo-Bronze age pillagers instead of smooth-faced burbanites. For the most informed appraisal of all, here's Julian's chat with Paradox about the game's procedural history generation - it writes you a latest apocalypse for every playthrough.

A post shared by 1- UP Gaming (@1upgaming03).

In a video posted to Instagram, for instance, we see a player casually walking into a jewelry store with a crate of beer under one arm and a swift right hook ready to go in the other. That's when Jason goes on a throwing spree, knocking out staff with some well-placed projectiles to the head and dusting up those who get a little close. Aside from a very brief alarm from a locked door, the robbery goes smoothly.

A post shared by Kotov GTA6 стримы (@kotov.plays).

A faster, less flash example shows a quick and easy shop robbery where a casual bottle to the bloke behind the counter allows for rapid access to the cash in the till. Whether bottles can be utilised for something more complicated, like a full-on bank heist, remains to be seen.

Recent findings suggest that bottles, though, are just the tip of the iceberg. Roadkill and random lizards on the street also make for handy non-lethal projectiles. Beer remains the more compelling option, however. In gun terms, beer crates have up to six rounds in their 'magazine', making them a reliable single source of stuff to throw at folks.

If you want to try this out yourself, Eurogamer's guide on GTA 6 robberies can get you started. Otherwise, our full GTA 6 walkthrough will take you even further through Rockstar's blockbuster release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While the fifth Toy Story gave us more insight into Jessie, it also gave us an insane Buzz Lightyear moment that was "heaven" for Tim Allen. The actor is known for his ad-libbing, both in his stand-up and in his sitcoms. Some of his best bits and impressions have made it on screen, and this goes for the toy-centric franchise as well. So naturally when the actor returned for the fifth movie, he saw an opportunity to improvise, but the Toy Story animators hated to see him coming.

It has been revealed that allen stopped by The Tonight Show to dish on all things Toy Story 5, and even answered Jimmy Fallon’s questions about that Buzz Lightyear army moment. The actor was totally on board with voicing 50 characters, but he admits that his excitement received mixed reactions from the animators:.

In a recent development, the problem with a comedian is that I’m in there doing bits. I’m talking to a foam ball. ‘Cause there’s no other actors, you know? So I’m doing this whole thing and every time you ad-lib in a Toy Story movie, the people have two reactions: ‘oh, that’s funny,’ and next is, ‘darn it.’ Because they’ve already animated some of it, so if I ad-lib they gotta go back and re-do it. So they don’t really like it, but they do like it.

The actor has been playing the character since the first Toy Story in 1995, and has given Buzz a specific voice that can be "deceptively hard to capture" for writers. So Allen gives the character a little something extra that has paid off in his favor, especially since we can thank the actor for an iconic moment:.

According to recent reports, the one I did that I loved. He said, ‘You are a toy!’ And I shut - I said, ‘You are a sad strange little man and you have my pity.’ And that was an ad-lib. They went, ‘Oh God, that’s good. Oh…’.

Industry observers note that it’s hard to imagine Toy Story without that moment. Though I can see how that would be frustrating for the animators. Ironically one wish that Allen had nearly came true. He has admitted that he wanted more Buzz, as he felt the character didn't have much in prior films. Allen has jokingly said this way people won’t remember “a fabric cowboy.”.

In fact, the actor almost got his wish as Toy Story 5 nearly didn’t have Woody at all. Though we did get a sweet reunion between the pals that would have been missed. While voicing so many parts at once sounds intimating, that’s not how Allen saw it:.

Sources indicate that I was in heaven, because there were 50 of me. So they run out, and then he goes, ‘We gotta go this way. We’re Space Rangers.’ The guy at the front. So I ad-libbed the two in the back. I wanted to go, ‘Why is he the leader? How come I can’t be leader?’ The other one goes, ‘Because he’s a Space Ranger and we’re all Space Rangers.’ And then he went back and forth. ‘I see no sign of intelligent life anywhere.’ ‘I see no…’ And I’m laughing my ass off in the studio. The window people are going, ‘No.’ We didn’t get one ad-lib in that thing.

Recent findings suggest that however, this wasn’t the first time we’ve seen a multi-Lightyear performance. There was a moment in Toy Story 2 with several Space Ranger toys on the shelves in Al’s Toy Barn. Then we spent some time with an alternative Buzz who temporarily took our Buzz’s place. Though we hadn’t seen a multi-toy arc quite to this extent, which was everything Allen wanted it to be and more.

Industry observers note that it’s unknown whether we’ll see another Toy Story, or if Allen (or Hanks) would return for a sixth, but a time existed when the third was going to be the last. As long as the story is there, and a chance to improv multiple Buzz Lightyears, I think the actor can easily be swayed back to the sound booth.

10 Hidden Controls Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You can have a ton of fun in GTA 6 even if you only follow the core gameplay loop of running around, stealing cars, and completing missions and side quests.
  • According to recent reports, if you just want to sit back and relax as your character drives around Leonida in GTA 6, you should try the auto-drive mode.
  • Recent findings suggest that your character is going to commit a lot of crimes in GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can have a ton of fun in GTA 6 even if you only follow the core gameplay loop of running around, stealing cars, and completing missions and side quests. However, if you take a minute to learn a few hidden controls, I think you'll enjoy the game even more. These are fairly simple controls that let you hide from the cops, trash talk other drivers, or flip the bird when you're feeling like annoying NPCs. These are 10 of the best hidden GTA 6 controls that'll help you unlock an entirely new side of the game.

According to recent reports, if you just want to sit back and relax as your character drives around Leonida in GTA 6, you should try the auto-drive mode. It's a relaxing way to enjoy the streets without having to worry about following traffic rules. To enable it, you need to get in a vehicle and add a waypoint on the map. This serves as your character's destination, so if you want a longer drive, be sure to drop the waypoint far, far away. Next, hold the down arrow on the D-Pad, and press the Option button. This enables cinematic mode. Then, hold the Circle button to enable auto-drive.

Recent findings suggest that your character is going to commit a lot of crimes in GTA 6. When this happens, you attract heat, and soon enough, cops will begin chasing you. Switching cars is a great way to reduce the amount of attention you get from law enforcement, but you can still be identified by your face or clothing. Until you can reach a safe spot to swap outfits, maintain a low profile by ducking while driving. Hold the Circle button while driving to duck.

According to recent reports, EA's Road Rash was among the first racing games I played as a child, and I remember how much fun it was to kick your rivals while speeding through the game's various courses. You can have a taste of that in GTA 6 too. Press the Square button while you're riding a bike, and your character will kick anyone who's near you. If you do this in a car, it opens the door, and hits people around the car. To annoy other drivers, press R3, and your character will direct some trash talk towards NPCs.

Hold Circle to lean back against walls, or to sit on the beach. To rest on a ledge, you can hold L3. This lets you take a moment to soak in beautiful views in the game, or lounge around as you listen to NPC conversations. Paying attention to those conversations can lead to some fun side quests, and sometimes give you a tip or two for quick money or other rewards.

Sources indicate that if you really want to rile people up in GTA 6, you can flip the bird. This works only when your character is unarmed. Hold L2, focus on a person, then press R1. Actions have consequences in GTA 6, so be prepared to fight NPCs when you do this.

When you're being chased by cops, enemies, or angry NPCs, you can use a quick shortcut to look back without turning the camera around. Just hold R3 to look behind you.

According to recent reports, while driving, press Circle to toggle headlights (and switch to high beams). This is particularly useful when you're offroading at night. You can also hold left arrow on the D-Pad, and move the right stick up to access other vehicle controls like hazard lights, opening or closing windows, etc., in case you want to add to the realism.

Stealing emergency vehicles in GTA 6 is risky, but the reward is totally worth it. Not only do you find stashes of weapons, gear, and money in some of these vehicles, but you also have access to sirens that help you clear traffic off your path. If you steal an ambulance or a cop car, hold L3, and move the left stick up to go through different siren tones. Press L3 and the left stick up to enable the siren.

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is a third-person game, but it has a first-person mode that partially works. It is useful for looking at smaller objects around your character, such as posters, small signs, or to look for clues in and around a house. (Yes, I am talking about Mandy's creepy house and bad vibes.) Hold L2 + hit R3 to switch to first-person mode. Sadly, you can't move when you do this, but you can look around. Try it in Mandy's property to observe a few nasty surprises.

Industry observers note that when you sprint towards a car, press the X button to slide across the hood. This is much faster and smoother than running around parked cars or jumping over them. It also looks cool, which is reason enough to try this feature.
