#212110. Organization of Heroes 3: Operation Torch review - moments of barely held-together chaos squandered by mechanical scripting

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (999 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Organization of Heroes 3: Operation Torch review - moments of barely held-together chaos squandered by mechanical scripting

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that after waiting three years for Relic to expand Company of Heroes 3's singleplayer, watching DLC after DLC focused on expanding the roster of units available in multiplayer matches, Operation Torch looks like a welcome addition.
  • Sources indicate that having played through the whole thing, I really want to say it's been worth the wait.
  • About halfway through the campaign, I'm put in charge of managing a retreat under a German advance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that after waiting three years for Relic to expand Company of Heroes 3's singleplayer, watching DLC after DLC focused on expanding the roster of units available in multiplayer matches, Operation Torch looks like a welcome addition. It's a new 15-mission campaign set in North Africa. following two US officers as they try to break the German Afrika Korps' hold on the region.

Sources indicate that having played through the whole thing, I really want to say it's been worth the wait. Unfortunately, it's not so straightforward as that.

About halfway through the campaign, I'm put in charge of managing a retreat under a German advance. While I must use my limited forces to hold back enemy troops at the head of the map, I'm also to drive a supply truck to different structures on the map so its crew can evacuate the buildings. It's a fraught start to the mission, forcing me to balance my attentions on the embattled front while also keeping a watchful eye on the vulnerable supply truck. German forces are seeping past the line and it would only take one well-placed anti-tank gun to spell an end to the evacuation.

The tension that comes in those moments, where I'm hopping about the battlefield barely holding things together, is Company of Heroes at its best. Operation Torch has several moments that reach that height of trying to command chaos, but they're squandered just as swiftly as they come.

When the three structures are broken down, I'm ordered to pull back to a hill outside of town. The mission isn't over, though: German officers are sifting through the abandoned buildings, looking for intel that was missed in the evacuation, and I'm to take two squads of snipers into enemy territory to kill them before they find anything. While it sounds exciting on paper, the mechanics of the mission's scripting make the reality underwhelming. My weakened army is sitting on a hill outside of town but no Germans come their way. In town, German units either stand still or travel in small looping patrols. Navigating the camouflaged sniper squads between them is easy work, but slow going. And even when they come out of stealth to shoot the officers and are spotted by a unit of German soldiers, they walk away from the fight and the Germans don't give chase. This may all be because I'm playing on standard difficulty, but the AI is oddly passive throughout Operation Torch.

Across multiple missions, I repeatedly used the same cheesing tactic. I would send a unit with the stealth passive to hide invisibly behind cover near the enemy, with strict orders not to open fire. With my infiltrator acting as a forward spotter, I'd then pummel the enemy with mortars from a safe distance. This tactic worked again and again. I knew, really, that it was no fun to do – turning every battle into a slow grinding down of the enemy – but it was also too effective to ignore when the enemy would never fight back.

It's a shame so many of Operation Torch's missions hit a bum, overly-scripted note because I really enjoyed their unfurling narrative. Admittedly, my military history is poor, and all my knowledge of the North Africa campaign is drawn from the bits in SAS Rogue Heroes before they go to Europe, but my general understanding is that it was a campaign that saw rapid advances turn into just-as-quick retreats. This plays into Operation Torch's missions where success often isn't pushing the front forwards, but holding the line while covering routed allied forces, or defending a pass long enough for air support to arrive and cause enough damage to force the Germans to slow down. And, because you're battling backwards and forwards over the same territory, Relic employ one of my favourite RTS tricks: throwing you back into the same map but from a different perspective. In one mission you may be on the assault, prizing free the Afrika Korps' grip on a town street by street, but then a few missions later you find yourself defending the same territory from a retaliatory attack. It's unfortunate that the same push and pull isn't as evident on the battlefield.

Industry observers note that relic are experimenters, often reinventing a game's systems between entries in a series or trying out a fresh mechanic in their expansions. In Operation Torch, the new toy is a choice of unlocks at the end of each mission. After a tank-focused assignment, for instance, you're offered a choice between a passive perk that makes Shermans 25% harder to hit while moving, or another which unlocks a different Sherman variant in your motor pool. Complete the map's optional objective and you also get to choose between a 10% reduction in tank costs and an upgrade that sees all your tanks produced at level 3 veterancy. These perks then apply throughout your campaign. By the final mission, the right side of your screen is a fat stack of passive and active perks. It's a neat idea but, in practice, it didn't seem to make a dramatic difference to how I played. I do like the idea of gradually developing your forces capabilities over a campaign but perhaps the difference needs to be more dramatic. Making your tanks slightly cheaper or harder to hit doesn't make that much of a tangible difference when you're right in there amidst the tracks and trenches.

Thus, it really does fall back to the strength of Operation Torch's missions, which are sometimes great but too often a case of rolling over the enemy very, very slowly. Perhaps this is a game best played with the difficulty whacked up high.

While I was hoping for more from Operation Torch, mind, I do hope it's not the last time we see Relic flesh out Tech giant of Heroes 3's singleplayer. There's still plenty of scope there, and plenty of room for further experiments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.
  • Industry observers note that it’s True Colors, from Latest York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Industry observers note that it’s True Colors, from Latest York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

One thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in Newly introduced York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Industry observers note that speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

Industry observers note that we’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this problem: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian.

In a recent development, van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

According to recent reports, honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

Sources indicate that so who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of Newly introduced York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is currently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

Sources indicate that the $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

— As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

Industry observers note that the 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

Sources indicate that — Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

Industry observers note that — The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred said the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”.

— For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

— Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. According to recent reports, nvidia may have finally released a proper cure for their last graphics driver, 621.24, reportedly writing unneccesarily vast amounts of data to some owners' SSDs. A hotfix late last week seemed to have made things better, but not fixed everything. Here's hoping driver 621.40 has managed to totally rectify things.

Alongside delivering enhancements specifically aimed at Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4, Where Winds Meet, and Assetto Corsa Rally, 621.40 lists dealing with the fact "excessive writes to file nvlog.nvlgstg may occur in background" as one of its key aims.

As to whether or not it's achieved that, some folks on Reddit and the Nvidia forum look to be making yes-shaped noises, but I'd not quite classify what I've seen so far as 100% proof. If you've reverted to the last driver which looked problem free, 621.01, waiting a few more days and seeing if a more definitive consensus emerges might be the best option.

It has been revealed that after all, the hotfix which preceded 621.40 also declared war against those excessive writes to file nvlog.nvlgstg, and it ended up stopping the excessive writing from starting right after you boot up and reducing the amount that's written, but not totally getting rid of the problem if an affected PC was left running for extended periods. At the very least, the fact the attempts at fixing the problem have now made their way into Nvidia's main branch is a key step towards the latest driver to hit the manufacturer's site and app eventually being excessive write-free.

As we've noted in our previous coverage of the matter, which doesn't seem to be affecting all machines, if you want to check if you're suffering from the excessive writing you'll need to open task manager, head to the 'details' tab, right click on the column header, click 'select columns', select 'I/O write bytes' from the menu of check boxes that brings up, then look for 'NVDisplay.Container.exe'. The number next that exe is in bytes, so you'll need to do some maths to work out if it's writing little scraps of MB or big bits of GB.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you use Signal, it's likely you care at least a little bit about keeping your communication private so only you and those you're chatting with can see your message threads.
  • Sources indicate that in a recent blog post, Signal president Meredith Whitaker outlined the potential threat AI assistants like Siri and Gemini pose to the platform's promise of privacy.
  • Signal has already blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI, which by default was able to take and store screen grabs of Signal messages on Windows 11.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you use Signal, it's likely you care at least a little bit about keeping your communication private so only you and those you're chatting with can see your message threads. Signal's end-to-end encryption keeps prying eyes out, but if you use agentic AI on your device, your chats may not be as locked down as you think.

Sources indicate that in a recent blog post, Signal president Meredith Whitaker outlined the potential threat AI assistants like Siri and Gemini pose to the platform's promise of privacy. Systems-level capabilities like Gemini Intelligence (on Android) and Siri AI's Onscreen Awareness (on iOS and macOS) scan your screen and may be able to capture data from Signal conversations in the process, which can then be used to perform tasks. Not only does this potentially expose your information, but that of other conversation participants as well. Whitaker notes that this leaves privacy protections outside of Signal's control because the platform cannot easily restrict AI access to the app.

Signal has already blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI, which by default was able to take and store screen grabs of Signal messages on Windows 11. While Signal cannot guarantee that AI won't have access to your data, there are a few protections now available for those on iOS and Android as well.

It has been revealed that the main workaround in Signal for now is to restrict screenshots and screen recordings inside the app, though this does not prevent AI agents from potentially grabbing content from other parts of your device. According to Signal's support documents, these protections will now be enabled by default on iOS 27 and Android with the latest versions of the Signal app.

Users on iOS 27 can confirm or manually disable screenshot protection via Settings > Privacy > Block Siri AI. The compromise with this setting is that it also blocks you from taking screenshots of Signal conversations in the app and App Switcher, though you can disable it temporarily for 10 minutes if needed. On Android, Signal automatically engages the "Screen security" setting when it detects an AI agent attempting to access the screen. This, too, blocks screenshots inside the app and can be disabled via Settings > Privacy > App security > Screen security. Signal cannot block screenshots on macOS 27. However, users can add Signal to their Excluded Apps list via System Settings > Siri, which at least limits proactive access to conversations by Siri AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6's launch took a massive bite out of Call of Duty’s player base, according to latest estimates from Alinea Analytics, and four days on, it still hasn't recovered.

Writing in Alinea's newsletter, Rhys Elliott said Call of Duty HQ's daily active users (DAUs) across PlayStation, Xbox, and Steam fell 42 percent when GTA 6 launched on 19th November, dropping from an average of 7.5 million to 4.4 million. On PlayStation, which Elliott describes as "CoD's main platform", the drop was 44 percent.

"Sadly, CoD has barely bounced back after four days," Elliott wrote. "It's still down 41% from its baseline.".

Fortnite and FC 27 took a hit too, but both are already recovering. Fortnite's DAUs on PlayStation and Xbox fell 28 percent, from 17.8 million to 12.8 million, but by the end of the weekend it had clawed its way back to 19 percent below its baseline.

Epic is also holding a live event to close out the current season on 5th December, which Elliott says the studio "hopes will pull players back after they’ve polished off GTA 6’s story".

FC 27's DAUs dropped by around 27 percent, from 5.9 million to 4.3 million, and it's already back within 20 percent of its baseline.

GTA 6's launch hit Call of Duty HARD (@alineaanalytics estimates).COD HQ's daily active consumers across PlayStation, Xbox, and Steam are down 42% from an average of 7.5M DAUs to 4.4M. On PlayStation – CoD’s main platform – Call of Duty took a 44% hit. Sadly, CoD has barely bounced… pic.twitter.com/XLa6N9TBfr.

According to Alinea, of those who'd played GTA 6 by the end of its launch weekend, 29 percent had also played Fortnite this month, 16 percent had played Call of Duty HQ, and 11 percent had played FC 27.

Industry observers note that elliott remarked the pattern is largely what Alinea had predicted: the major live service games took an instant hit from GTA, but bounced back "because they're ingrained habits". Call of Duty is "the outlier here", he added, "and Xbox should - candidly - be worried about one of its premier franchises".

Elliott also points out that all of this is the impact of GTA 6's single-player mode. He expects its online component and PC port to arrive "some time next year", and when they do, he indicates, "the bounce back will not be so obtainable".

Alinea also estimates that GTA 6 has sold 44.9 million copies and made more than $4 billion since launch.

According to recent reports, GTA 6 debuted on Thursday, 19th November, for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. While it's the biggest entertainment launch of all time, selling 32.5 million pre-release copies and making $3.79 billion by the end of its first day, you wouldn't know it from its Metacritic user score, as players review bomb it over its limited FPS and purported "woke" agenda.

Sources indicate that eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. If you need help getting through the game now that it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough and a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

"Clearly not everything has gone well" during Fable's lengthy creation, says Playground boss, but the "original vision" remains intact despite taking cues from other RPGs

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Fable reboot is finally set to kick the release chicken (I'm not sure that's an established phrase anywhere in the world, but roll with it) early next year, following a not small amount of time in development and multiple delays.
  • I say this with some pride – tempered against the fact that this has been obviously an enormously long development, so clearly not everything has gone well – but I would say that our original vision of what Fable needs to be has remained unchanged," Ralph Fulton, one of Playground's co-founders, told our suit-wearing siblings at GIBiz.
  • "There are many reasons that this game development has been long," he added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Fable reboot is finally set to kick the release chicken (I'm not sure that's an established phrase anywhere in the world, but roll with it) early next year, following a not small amount of time in development and multiple delays. Despite that long time in the oven having made it necessary to look beyond just the series' classic entries for RPG inspiration, Playground Games' Fable general manager has noted the team's "original vision" of what a Fable game needs to be hasn't changed.

I say this with some pride – tempered against the fact that this has been obviously an enormously long development, so clearly not everything has gone well – but I would say that our original vision of what Fable needs to be has remained unchanged," Ralph Fulton, one of Playground's co-founders, told our suit-wearing siblings at GIBiz.

"There are many reasons that this game development has been long," he added. "It's a newly introduced team, it's a new genre, a new franchise, new technology – although we're building in an engine that we know well. It's also because a Fable game must have a great story with memorable characters and high-stakes drama, and also it needs to be funny and to have that British wit infused throughout it. Then there's combat, the quest structure, and the world of Albion and its people, and the simulations that underpin it. You'd be nuts to take on all of that in the first project, and yet here we are.".

Fulton went on to note that despite that, Playground have worked to ensure their game's scope hasn't grown ever wider as they've made it. One call made early on with the social and economic simming that goes with the likes of landlording and being a dick to entire villages was that the studio "would only model first and second degree ripple effects", due to feeling that "players would only notice or we could only communicate the consequences up to the second degree". That makes sense, not every game can or should be a strategy game like Civ, wherein seeing your actions cause or influence a thousand different tidal waves over time is part of the central appeal. Not every game also has the budget of a GTA 6, which works deep simulation mechanics into a crime adventure, but feels like an exception to the rules even compared to Xbox-backed games like Fable.

On the other hand, Fulton did make clear that Playground have looked beyond the original entries in the series for RPG inspiration, fearing their game might be left behind if not. "Principally, technology has advanced," he noted when asked what's changed while the game's been in the works. "In 2015, The Witcher 3 redefined what an open-world action RPG looks like and became the gold standard. And after that bar was raised, the Assassin's Creed franchise changed into this more modern iteration with Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla, and became like a quasi-RPG.

"All of these games continue to reset player expectations, which means I think looking only to the original Fable trilogy for inspiration would leave us lacking in terms of what the modern audience, the modern marketplace, expects.".

Recent findings suggest that we've already seen some of the ways in which the reboot diverges from its older forebears. As far as I'm concerned, albeit as someone with only a brief dalliance in the classic Fables, such tweaks could go either way. It is interesting to see Assassin's Creed mentioned alongside The Witcher 3 as having changed the RPG game. A game like Baldur's Gate 3 or even Starfield would strike me as a more obvious candidate to point to, so the AC mention might offer some indiction of the direction Playground have taken with their design.

Fable is, of course, being backed by Microsoft. The company are subject to an ongoing boycott by the BDS movement and have inflicted significant layoffs on their Xbox studios this year. As for whether the latter upheaval has affected Playground or Xbox's backing of Fable, Fulton offered a rather nothing answer here about Forza Horizon being good for the studio and the importance of keeping everyone internally in the loop as to how work on the game's going.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CD Projekt Red has said people can expect a similar qualitative and technological leap from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 as has been witnessed between Grand Theft Auto 5 and Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski made the remark during a Q3 earnings call this afternoon, during which he and CDPR faced a handful of questions related to GTA 6.
  • "First of all, obviously this is a call about us, not about Rockstar," Nowakowski began by saying, "but I do understand the connection here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CD Projekt Red has said people can expect a similar qualitative and technological leap from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 as has been witnessed between Grand Theft Auto 5 and Grand Theft Auto 6.

CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski made the remark during a Q3 earnings call this afternoon, during which he and CDPR faced a handful of questions related to GTA 6.

"First of all, obviously this is a call about us, not about Rockstar," Nowakowski began by saying, "but I do understand the connection here. Having said that, I'm not going to make a deep-dive and a full-blown review of GTA 5 versus GTA 6. But of course we did look at the game, we did see the differences.

In a recent development, "We believe there's going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4 - I think so, yes. It's been 11 years, we are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game, so yes you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4.".

Another question was about whether GTA 6 had affected development aims for The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2 - a question well-timed after Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzynski joked at the weekend that "Cyberpunk 2 is cancelled" because of how impressive GTA 6 is.

"Is seeing GTA 6 launch making us make the games more expensive?" stated Nowakowski. "We have certain ambitions when it comes to Witcher [4] and Cyberpunk 2; they have not changed when it comes to GTA 6. If anything happened as a result of GTA 6, it's [that it's] always great to see games like that because they show you how much cool stuff can be done, and that's for sure an inspiration in many ways for our developers.".

Specifically in terms of budget, Nowakowski noted nothing had changed, and also echoed a point made earlier this year when he said Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2 are "not budget-driven developments".

It has been revealed that "I'm not saying we don't care about the budgets: we do, and I'm pretty sure [Rockstar] did as well. But you cannot make games like that having in mind 'this is the fixed number of money I want to spend and that's it, otherwise I'm gone'," he stated.

"They're ambition-driven developments and money's notable - the budgets are not indefinite, that's not what we're saying. But the philosophy is like I said, and honestly that philosophy has not changed for us because of GTA 6's release; it has just always been like that.".

Industry observers note that when asked whether the arrival of GTA 6 had impacted sales of The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077, Nowakowski answered "yes and no". "You do see a certain dip in engagement on the PlayStation and Xbox for sure," he remarked.

Statistics apparently show a drop of "at least" 25 percent in CDPR's players as they "engaged themselves with GTA 6". "But you do have to remember that a lot of our players are PC-based," Nowakowski pointed out. "GTA has not rolled out on PC; we have not seen any impact whatsoever on the PC sales or engagement. So it's a bit of a mixed answer.

"And also on the PS5 and Xbox, it's not like our sales came to zero," he added. "Some short impact, yes, on the consoles. Long-term, we do not really see that affecting ourselves in any material way in Q4.".

According to recent reports, finally, the questioning turned to marketing, which Rockstar has shown can reach far and wide if you have the brand-power of GTA and some imagination. We've seen prestigious department stores like Selfridges taken over by Rockstar for GTA 6, trailers premiering on Netflix, Miami launch festivals - Rockstar's marketing department has gone all out.

CDPR is no stranger to grabbing headlines with glitzy actor hirings such as Keanu Reeves, but will Rockstar's approach to marketing GTA 6 push it a step further?

"The most crucial takeaway - I'm not sure if I'd call it a lesson because this is our playbook as well - is that if you want to reach a certain critical mass, you do have to get out of just the core gaming bubble, something we did in the past as well," Nowakowski said. "For sure, GTA 6 went there.

It has been revealed that "If the underlying question was if we're going to repeat or copy-paste their playbook: no, for sure not. Our games are different and they require a certain different approach - we just do things differently than they do. But in terms of the ultimate effect, in terms of breaking out to the mass market awareness: this is for sure something we consider pivotal to whatever we're going to do with our marketing campaigns in the future.".

CDPR's Q3 financial results were positive. The organization made less money than this time last year, but the "fresh momentum" - as Nowakowski put it - provided to The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 by the release of the Remastered edition of Witcher 3 and the Edgerunners anime series on Netflix, and associated game revision, went a long way.

The Witcher 3 reached its highest concurrent player count on Steam as a result, and Cyberpunk 2077 reached its second highest concurrent player count, which represents serious staying power for both games so long after they were first released. And with Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past on track for 2027, and The Witcher 4 for 2028, the future is loaded.

Tech Report: Two Budget Smartwatches That Make Perfect Gifts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you or someone on your shopping list wants a new smartwatch, you have plenty of options to choose from.
  • Sources indicate that luckily, you do have options.
  • Contrary to what you might expect, Amazfit has no ties to Amazon—other than that you can buy these watches from the latter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you or someone on your shopping list wants a new smartwatch, you have plenty of options to choose from. The problem is, a lot of them can be quite pricey. Apple's cheapest smartwatch, the SE 3, starts at $249, and its other selections only skyrocket from there. On the flip side, the risk in picking a smartwatch that's too inexpensive is that the manufacturer likely made a series of sacrifices to get the price that low. At a certain point, the tradeoff just isn't worth it.

Sources indicate that luckily, you do have options. There are two smartwatches on the market that aren't just cheaper than the competition, they're not even in the same ballpark. And while you shouldn't expect the same capabilities as you would on flagship wearables, these devices are perfectly usable, both as fitness trackers and smartwatches—all while spending well below $100 a pop. CNET put both smartwatches through their paces to make these determinations, so you know whichever model you get, you won't be picking up a wearable paperweight.

Contrary to what you might expect, Amazfit has no ties to Amazon—other than that you can buy these watches from the latter. Amazfit is its own organization, and produces a wide selection of smartwatch options. The Bip 6 happens to be the company's latest budget smartwatch, with an MSRP of just $79.99. In most cases, a price that low would be a red flag for a smartwatch, but not in the Bip 6's case.

The Amazfit Bip 6 holds its own against other flagship smartwatches. That's true on a surface level: This watch looks your average smartwatch, rather than a cheap imitation. In fact, at first glance, I'd bet most people would assume the Bip 6 is actually an Apple Watch. It has a rounded square design with a large 1.97-inch display with a resolution of 390 by 450 pixels (though there's no Always-On display). This isn't a cheap display, either: Amazfit put an AMOLED screen on the watch, which looks great indoors—though CNET Labs struggled to see the screen in direct sunlight.

Where the Bip 6 really shines, however, is with fitness tracking. This watch supports GPS, which makes tracking outdoor runs possible without a smartphone. CNET Labs found that it takes about 10 seconds to find a GPS signal, but once it connects, you're set. While running, the Bip 6 reliably tracks your heart rate. CNET Labs compared its sensor to the Polar chest strap HR monitor and found it on par, though, like other smartwatches, the Bip 6 is slower at detecting heart rate spikes. You'll get data like cadence and stride while tracking runs, and strength training and muscle groups while working out indoors. For example, CNET Labs found that it correctly identified arm muscle exercises while testing the watch during a pilates session.

You also get some health and wellness features, too. The Bip 6 can measure heart rate variations, body temperature changes, sleep stages, and even your breathing quality. Its One Tap Measuring mode supports a single reading for heart rate, SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation), stress, and breathing rate, and it supports cycle tracking—though CNET specifies it can't track skin temperature like other smartwatches and health trackers. There's an optional subscription that provides AI coaching tools and looks out for health conditions like sleep apnea and insomnia. While health and wellness tracking is solid, note that CNET Labs found Amazfit's app, Zepp, to be confusing, since it simply displays your data without much context or explanation.

For an $80 smartwatch, the Bip 6 has an excellent battery life. CNET Labs found that the watch could be pushed to its limits—multiple workouts using GPS, heart rate tracking, keeping the display on during workouts—and still run for eight days before needing a charge. In fact, reviewer Vanessa Hand Orellana speculates you could push the Bip 6 to Amazfit's two-week battery life claim by limiting some of the most intensive settings and features. The only downside here is that there is no fast charging, so it will take about two hours to get back to 100%. But if you're only charging the watch once every week or two, that isn't much of a burden. There's also no charger in the box, so you'll need to use a separate USB-C cable.

Recent findings suggest that as a smartwatch, the Bip 6 can be a mixed bag. CNET found that the UI was clunky and sluggish, and the OS requires some user intervention before it's as usable as a standard Apple Watch or Galaxy Watch. While the watch has a voice assistant, Flow, CNET found it to be borderline unusable. However, CNET says Android users can reply to texts with a keyboard or dictation without needing the assistant. iPhone users can't do the same by default, but by downloading a third-party app, they can jerry-rig the watch to send and receive texts.

In a recent development, based on CNET Labs' testing, the Amazfit Bip 6 is one of the best budget smartwatches you can buy. For $80, you get a reliable workout tracker that looks like most standard watches on the market. And while you're making some sacrifices at this price point, they're largely worth it for $80.

While the Amazfit is a good choice for both iPhone and Android owners, the Galaxy Fit 3 might be the best choice for Samsung users. This isn't an option for iPhone users, and while it works with all Android devices, you get some Samsung-specific perks if you have a Galaxy phone.

Sources indicate that the Galaxy Fit 3 is even cheaper than the Amazfit Bip 6: This watch is only $60, which makes it among the cheapest smartwatches you can buy. Now, this doesn't look like your average smartwatch. Samsung opted for a fitness tracker-like design, with a long 1.6-inch (40mm) AMOLED display. But for a fitness tracker/smartwatch hybrid, it's a solid look.

In a recent development, in CNET's testing, one of the Galaxy Fit 3's biggest strengths is its battery life—though it pales in comparison to the Bip 6. When pushed to its limits, the Fit 3 can run three days in between charges, though Samsung claims you can get it up to 13 days with the right settings. While the Amazfit has it beat, the Fit 3 might sound like a dream compared to other smartwatches, even from Samsung. Unlike the Bip 6, the Fit 3 supports fast charging. You can fill the watch up completely in just over an hour.

CNET did find that the "smart" elements of this wearable were a bit lacking, however. The Fit 3 doesn't support voice dictation or mobile payments like other watches do, and unless you have a Galaxy phone, you won't be able to access the camera remote or sync your alarms. And while the Amazfit Bip 6's "Flow" is hardly reliable, the Fit 3 doesn't have an assistant at all. You can see incoming calls and decline (but not answer) them, and you can send prewritten responses to text messages, but not initiate them. Still, CNET found that Samsung added the essentials: You have an alarm, calculator, weather app, camera remote, and, of course, the Samsung Health app. (What kind of health tracker would this be without it?).

CNET found that the Fit 3 is a reliable fitness tracker, particularly for $60. You can track over 100 different workouts, and the watch automatically logs exercises like runs, walks, rowing, and elliptical sessions—if you enable auto-tracking, that is. It also supports swimming with its IP68 water resistance rating. CNET Labs found that the heart rate tracking was "generally accurate" when compared to the Polar chest strap, though its slower with registering heart rate spikes. Interestingly, the heart rate tracker was a bit delayed in testing, but once CNET reviewed the data in the health app, the data had corrected to be largely accurate. You also get high and low heart rate alerts, though no ECG app. (The $249 Apple Watch SE 3 also omits this feature.).

According to recent reports, in CNET's testing, the sleep tracker on the Fit 3 was useful, if not entirely accurate. The watch can detect your sleep stages and look out for snoring using your Galaxy phone's mic. Like other health trackers, you get a sleep score, but CNET found it a bit inaccurate, since it rated a six and a half hour sleep session "Excellent" (91/100).

Still, the Fit 3 is really the only other smartwatch option at this price point that people should seriously consider. Until another company drops a product around this MSRP, you have two solid choices in the Amazfit Bip 6 and Galaxy Fit 3.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ubisoft, they of the recently revealed generative AI-focused game studio Motherbrain, have denied they're forcing upcoming games being pitched by their developers to integrate use of genAI as a rule.
  • The report from Vertical Slice cited anonymous Ubisoft staff as having said that the publishers' game pitching process now requires devs to either outline how they'll use generative AI to speed up production, or offer a specific justification as to why the tech isn't being used.
  • Ubisoft management reportedly revealed the change during a presentation to staff, with one source telling Vertical Slice that the manufacturer are all in on generative AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft, they of the recently revealed generative AI-focused game studio Motherbrain, have denied they're forcing upcoming games being pitched by their developers to integrate use of genAI as a rule. The publishers' statement comes in the wake of a report claiming that Ubisoft devs with pitches that don't use genAI are required to explain in detail why they've decided it isn't suitable for the game being outlined.

The report from Vertical Slice cited anonymous Ubisoft staff as having said that the publishers' game pitching process now requires devs to either outline how they'll use generative AI to speed up production, or offer a specific justification as to why the tech isn't being used.

Ubisoft management reportedly revealed the change during a presentation to staff, with one source telling Vertical Slice that the manufacturer are all in on generative AI. They cited an "attitude shift" among Ubisoft management as having left workers feeling "cornered by generative AI all the time", but made clear Ubisoft haven't brought in a blanket mandate forcing devs to use genAI no matter what.

Ubisoft have emphasised the latter in a statement subsequently issued to Vertical Slice. "We encourage our teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work," the company wrote. "This doesn’t mean that projects are required to use generative AI. Teams need to determine whether, and how, these technologies make sense for the game they want to make and the experience they want to create for players.".

Ubisoft have been keen on experimenting with genAI in game development for a little while - something essentially set in stone by the establishing of Motherbrain as a proper division where the manufacturer can work on the likes of the "first playable generative AI experience" they were shouting about earlier this year. That move came in a year Ubisoft have spent vast swaths of laying off staff and closing studios, as part of a restructuring they kicked off with a barrage of cancellations in January.

Most recently, those cuts hit 166 staff at Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, both of which worked on Assassin's Creed Shadows. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx, Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona, long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm, Ubisoft's Paris HQ and three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz are all on a list of other affected subsidiaries that I'm very much getting tired of wheeling out whenever Ubisoft inevitably insist on adding to it.

Changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

The Steam Awards turn 10 with throwback categories and a Game of the Year Hall of Fame

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nominations for the 2026 Steam Awards are now open, and to mark the event's 10th anniversary, Valve has brought back some categories from years past and added a Hall of Fame.
  • You've got until 6pm UK (10am Pacific) on 30th November to nominate your favourite games of the year across 14 categories.
  • The newly introduced Hall of Fame category will appear when voting opens, and will let players choose their favourite from Steam's previous Game of the Year winners to crown the best game of the past decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nominations for the 2026 Steam Awards are now open, and to mark the event's 10th anniversary, Valve has brought back some categories from years past and added a Hall of Fame.

You've got until 6pm UK (10am Pacific) on 30th November to nominate your favourite games of the year across 14 categories. Returning throwbacks include Just 5 More Minutes, Defies Description, and This is My Job Now, which recognises games that simulate mundane real-life jobs.

The newly introduced Hall of Fame category will appear when voting opens, and will let players choose their favourite from Steam's previous Game of the Year winners to crown the best game of the past decade.

Most categories are only open to games released on Steam since last year's Autumn Sale.

Recent findings suggest that the exception is the Labo(u)r of Love award, which goes to older games that developers are still supporting with latest content. Previous Labo(u)r of Love winners, including Warframe, Grand Theft Auto 5, Cyberpunk 2077, and Baldur's Gate 3, can't be nominated again.

According to recent reports, five finalists will be revealed in each category when voting opens alongside the Steam Winter Sale on 17th December. Voting closes at 10am Pacific on 2nd January, and the winners will be confirmed straight afterwards.

Nominating in at least one category also earns you the first level of Steam's Nomination Committee badge.

Earlier this month, Valve released a new Steam update that adds Steam Deck framerate data to a game's store page, giving potential buyers an indication of how well a game runs on the handheld.

Deborah Nevins—a Legend of Landscape Architecture—Plants With Purpose

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Upcoming York where we could imagine our future children growing up.
  • It looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale.
  • Our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Upcoming York where we could imagine our future children growing up. We looked upstate, in Connecticut, and at all those charming hamlets strung along the eastern end of Long Island known as the Hamptons. Toured hundreds of houses, clicked thousands of listings. But not one felt like home.

Nevins in her garden in East Hampton.

It looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale. A great furrowed trunk rising from a froth of flowering vines that split into enormous limbs sweeping improbably far across the garden. Its arrangement was so baroque—veiny, muscular wood twisting and reaching, dissolving overhead into a canopy of green delicacy. We could picture our children climbing its winding branches, little hands against its ridged, mossy bark.

Our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend. Now we joke that we didn’t buy a house—we bought this tree.

But what is it? A butternut tree? An oak? A black walnut? Deborah Nevins, one of the most revered living landscape designers, created this garden for the previous owners in 2004. In the fall, she invited me to her white-shingled cottage in Springs, East Hampton, to find out. Her living room has triple-hung windows like those in Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s house in Virginia, which go down to the floor so it’s easy to wheel in her potted lemon trees when the seasons change. “Winter is divine; it’s when they bloom,” she coos. “The house smells of lemon blossoms.”.

David Geffen’s pool at his former Beverly Hills estate, once home to Warner Bros.’ Jack Warner.

In a recent development, “Butternut!” she declares, slamming the book shut with all the force of her petite five-foot-nothing frame. “For sure.”.

Industry observers note that this is our tree. A butternut that likely sprouted generations before she came along. “It’s a native tree, probably a hundred years old. But I’d have to know the caliper—the diameter about a foot up—to be more precise.” She decided it’d be the anchor for our yard design the moment she saw it—existing mature trees are “sacred” and must be preserved at all costs. At its base, she dared to plant clematis, usually a climbing vine, that now rambles across the ground, softening the old tree’s trunk with a tangle of flowers. The butternut divides the rest of the property into distinct passages, including an ornamental reflecting pool bordered by hornbeam hedges, a lap pool shaded under locust trees, and a gravel path lined with rounded boxwoods.

GREEK MYTHOLOGY It took Nevins eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete her collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. What was once a parking lot is now planted with more than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs.

A rendering of the 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens.

To Nevins, the tree is an excellent example of her greater gardening philosophy: “I’m interested in creating unfolding spaces which intensify [the viewers’] experience, your sense of place and movement through a garden,” she claims. She frequently builds hedges and allées to control viewers’ attention, like horse blinders. “Not every aspect of the garden is seen at once. You have to stop and think.”.

Over the last four decades, Nevins has been entrusted with the grounds of some extraordinary spaces. Her clients include media mogul David Geffen, fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger, former Disney chairman Michael Eisner, and hotelier Ian Schrager. Commissions can range from tiny residential spaces (like mine) to huge commercial projects abroad. It took her eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete a 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens. That was a collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on a landscape that climbs over the buildings themselves, planted with native grasses from the hills of Attica and fragrant Mediterranean herbs, including lavender, rosemary, and oregano. Nevins’s mantra for the project was simple: “Speak Greek.” The execution was anything but simple. More than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs fill the public work. Nevins conceptualized the totality of the park. “I chose every single tree!” she states. “We had to propagate hundreds of thousands of plants throughout Greece, and we decided to hire various nurseries so that if there was a disease or fire, the entire crop would not be wiped out.” Her effort impressed Piano. “It is always special when, beyond the work on a project itself, you realize that you share the same values and ideas,” says Piano of Nevins, whom he describes as a “wonderful professional and human adventure.”.

“There is discipline in her work but never rigidity,” indicates Scott Mitchell, the West Coast–based architect who met Nevins at a dinner honoring architect Richard Meier in 1997 and went on to work with her on properties for Geffen in both California and Latest York. “Her landscapes don’t compete with architecture; they give it a place to belong.”.

He recalls the “emotional power” of her work for Geffen at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, former home of Warner Bros. cofounder Jack Warner. “Endless sweeps of white azaleas, a driveway lined with ancient, gnarled native sycamores, and 11 acres of rolling meadow beneath giant coast live oaks,” Mitchell says. “World-class projects require cohesion between architecture and landscape. They have to play from the same sheet of music. Debby totally gets that. Her response to architecture is clear and harmonious—confident but never overstepping.”.

Tommy Hilfiger and Dee Ocleppo at their Mustique estate.

Gil Schafer, a Fresh York–based architect who has worked with Nevins on more than 25 houses and gardens, also commends her command of structure. At his own house near Millbrook, she built a 12-foot-high hornbeam enclosure nestled into the surrounding farm fields that has, he states, “an almost abstract sculptural quality—as if Richard Serra had suddenly decided to work in hornbeam rather than Corten steel.”.

Industry observers note that nevins was born in Manhattan at what was then the Doctors Hospital on the Upper East Side. The family resided in the penthouse of the same building where Greta Garbo lived. Her father died of a brain tumor at 43, when Nevins was six months old, and so her mother had to return to work. At six, she was sent to Camp Taconic in Massachusetts. “I was tiny! My mother might have been arrested today.” She remembers walking in the woods, finding a strawberry, and reporting the discovery in a letter home. The seed had been planted—pun quite obvious.

Fleur Cowles, the formidable editor behind the short-lived, extravagantly inventive magazine Flair, was a maternal relative and had an outsize impact on her childhood. “She knew everyone, and she was so brilliant,” Nevins notes, offering me an issue of Flair from another bookshelf like a cherished family heirloom. Another influence was her mother’s sister, Miriam Sampson, an interior decorator who lived across from Carnegie Hall. “In this big apartment, she had her office in one room, and she had little models of apartments. I was so intrigued,” Nevins recalls. She’d cut out pictures of interiors and gardens from magazines and assemble them in scrapbooks. “But I didn’t even know about this idea of being a landscape architect.”.

When Nevins was 14, her mother remarried and the family moved to Fresh Haven, Connecticut. She went on to attend Boston University for undergrad and returned to New York for graduate school at Columbia. “They didn’t think that landscape history, which is what I wanted to study, was academic enough. And they probably had no one to teach it anyway,” she indicates. So she earned an MA and an MPhil in art history. Travel became a form of individualized study. “I learned by looking,” she says. She sought out Le Corbusier’s buildings in France, including La Tourette, Maisons Jaoul, and Villa Savoye, and drove from Paris to Santiago de Compostela looking at Romanesque and Merovingian churches. She made her first of many pilgrimages to Sissinghurst, a garden in Kent created by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her diplomat husband, Harold Nicolson. “There’s nothing more beautiful than Sissinghurst,” she sighs.

In a recent development, one of Nevins’s greatest champions has been Geffen, whom Victoria Newhouse, the renowned architecture critic and widow of longtime Condé Nast chairman Si Newhouse, introduced her to. On her first meeting with Geffen, Nevins arrived to present her work with a carousel of 80 slides. “After maybe 30 slides, he claims, ‘That’s enough. You’re hired.’ And I thought to myself, Who is this guy?” When she looked him up, she read that one of his attributes is spotting talent. “And that was that.”.

At the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, she removed one swimming pool to open up the landscape, built a upcoming one with a new patio house where Warner had a putting green, and relocated several mature oak trees on the property. “David is not afraid of major moves,” she says. (They preserved the fountains and terraces Warner had commissioned from Florence Yoch, who designed the grounds of Tara for Gone With the Wind, of course.) However, according to Nevins, when Warner’s daughter came to see what Geffen had done, she looked around and asked if they had changed anything. “ ‘What did we change? We changed everything!’ ” Nevins remembers Geffen saying. “The idea that we didn’t do a thing is crazy, but that it looked like it was meant to be—that’s a good thing. The ultimate compliment that looks like I did nothing.”.

An aerial view of Deborah Nevins’s Hamptons garden.

Hilfiger hired Nevins for a property in Mustique in the early 1990s, and again for his Denbigh Farm in Greenwich in 1995. In the Caribbean, she created palm promenades and a courtyard of white flowers; in Connecticut, she brought the elements of an old estate into a coherent whole. “I knew she was incredibly passionate about her work, and that always interested me because I love working with people who are passionate about what they do,” Hilfiger notes. “Her execution was impeccable, and she delivered exactly what she promised.”.

Nevins’s office is based in New York City, and she keeps between 5 and 10 new projects going at all times. “Almost any job is interesting unless I hear in advance that the people aren’t nice,” she says. “Also, art collectors, in my experience, have been great patrons. If you’re an art collector—and you’re truly not collecting just to make money from art—you have an interest in beauty and understanding.”.

Sources indicate that PLEACHY KEEN “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say,” architect Gil Schafer indicates of Nevins. “She feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

On average, it takes two years to get a garden up and running, three years if she needs to build upcoming structures. But a garden is never finished. Roberta Denning, who with her husband, Steve, commissioned Nevins for her family’s property in Greenwich in 2006, describes the pleasure of living with something that acquires depth while continuing to change. “What she created has grown more valuable with time,” Denning says of her property, which includes a walking labyrinth among chestnuts and beech trees. “Nearly 20 years on, the gardens feel both that they have always been here and that they are continually renewed.” Nevins says clients have joked that hiring her is like a marriage because it’s a long-term relationship, and it requires work. “So I guess I’m a polygamist?” she smiles.

Recent findings suggest that patience is a significant part of her process. “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say, and this is one way that we are so similar in our approach,” Schafer indicates. “You need to give her the space to read the land and sort out how she wants to approach it. I think she also feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

People joke that Nevins speaks to the plants, but Schafer isn’t sure it’s an act. “I think she really does!”.

In a recent development, “I do love them,” Nevins claims of her botanical family. “I was at a nursery with someone the other day, and I remarked, ‘It’s problematic. I get crushes on plants, but sometimes they don’t really have a place, and it’s so disappointing. It’s like a failed romance.’”.

A walking labyrinth in Greenwich, Connecticut.

Industry observers note that presently her crush is Stewartia pseudocamellia. “It has amazing bark, and the flower looks like a camellia, but it’s not a camellia, it’s a tree.” One plant she doesn’t love? Flowering forsythia, which Schafer reports she often refers to as “spring vomit.”.

In a recent development, nevins believes her greatest asset is the ability to blend both architectural history and botanical skill. “I have such a strong academic background in architectural history,” she notes. “I know exactly what these references are that they make to historical, even modern historical buildings.”.

Recent findings suggest that in another part of Long Island, Nevins combined the elements into what she calls a “beech house”—pun absolutely intentional. Martin Filler, an architecture critic and longtime contributor to The New York Review of Books, met Nevins when they were graduate students in Columbia’s art history department in the early 1970s. At the time, his wife, Rosemarie Haag Bletter, an architectural historian and professor emerita of art history at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City, was working on her PhD and teaching undergraduates. According to Filler, Nevins promised back then to design them a garden one day. “Since we didn’t have a house and never expected to, we said to ourselves, ‘Yeah, right,’ ” he claims. “But who knew that someday we would, and that gardening would become such a large part of our lives, especially Rosemarie’s?”.

Sources indicate that in the mid-1990s, they bought a cottage that had been part of Stanford White’s Breese estate, The Orchard, in Southampton. “Debby stated that she would now make good on her promise to design a garden for us,” Filler remembers. “By that time she had become one of the top landscape designers, but she insisted on doing it and refused to be paid.” She stayed with them for a winter weekend and spent hours walking the property. “Then she sat down at our dining table with a roll of yellow tracing paper and the surveyor’s map, and she designed the whole thing within a few hours. She joked, ‘Don’t tell anyone how fast I was.’ ”.

THE GIVING TREE When Derek C. Blasberg first saw the majestic tree in the backyard of a property in the Hamptons, he knew he’d found a home for his family. The hunt to identify it led him to Nevins’s larger body of work. “We could picture our children climbing its winding branches.”.

The Beech House, a 16-foot-by-16-foot-by-16-foot living gazebo made of 26 purple beech trees (Fagus sylvatica “Dawyck Purple”), is the centerpiece. The trees were sourced from Buffalo, trucked to Southampton, and replanted in the same orientation in which they had been grown. (“Each tree had to be marked with a dot of blue paint to indicate due north and then planted in that same geographical direction,” Filler remembers.) They were wired and trained over a wooden inner framework shaped like the schematic outline of a house and then clipped into shape on the exterior. The floor was paved with bluestone squares and rectangles in a random-looking pattern Nevins designed.

“Each year when we meet with our accountant to do our tax return, he’s always shocked that we spend so much on the garden,” Filler notes. “We tell him: ‘You have clients who have boats, you have clients who have classic cars—well, this is our pleasure, our indulgence.’”.

An apology from RPS

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (397 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday I made a significant error in judgement.
  • My failures towards you were several.
  • Industry observers note that secondly, for mentioning you at all in the apology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday I made a significant error in judgement. In writing an apology to our readers, I made a target of one of our writers and I won't be able to undo that. What I can try to do is apologise to that writer, who I'm addressing now.

My failures towards you were several. Firstly, in not explaining that we are able to step in by replying to and moderating comments when a discussion is becoming heated or aggressive, I never made it clear there were protections available to you that you weren't receiving.

Industry observers note that secondly, for mentioning you at all in the apology. While I hoped to make it clear to readers we wouldn't disrespect them in future, I laid the blame for that on your feet in public. The responsibility of an editor is to protect their writers, and I failed you profoundly.

Thirdly, that I didn't speak to you ahead of the post. As far as you were concerned the matter was settled, and I then put it in public without any warning.

Sources indicate that fourth, while we often talk of RPS being a collection of different writers with different viewpoints, where no one member of the team has the definitive view on a subject, this creates a vacuum for our contributors to operate in. This means new writers have very little direction when it comes to how they approach any topic and the response their work may receive. Again, any failings here are ultimately my responsibility.

Finally, this failure is all the more significant because it has happened across lines of gender privilege. RPS has a full-time staff of cisgender men, which inevitably gives rise to bias and ignorance we must actively confront, while we work towards being in a position to address our lack of gender diversity, beyond commissioning the occasional marginalised freelance writer. Non-cisgender writers are both much more exposed to abuse and much less favoured in terms of steady work. As such, a public rebuke from your own editor is far more damaging than it would be if the freelancer were a cisgender man. On this count, I have been extremely thoughtless in ways that would likely not have been the case when this site had a majority female editorship.

Ashley, I am deeply sorry that I let you down in these ways.
